sessions.title: Payoff-table anatomy: stake, gross payoff, net payoff & terminal wealth
sessions.focus: Translate a finite game into probabilities, gross payoffs, net payoffs and terminal wealth.
sessions.purpose: Prevent accounting ambiguity before any expectation or decision calculation.
sessions.centralCapability: Validate the outcome probabilities of a finite game. Distinguish gross payoff from net payoff after an entry stake.
sessions.principalObstacle: Gross prize, profit and terminal bankroll are often treated as the same number.

sessions.transferScope: A changed game surface requiring the same quantitative reasoning while preserving the stated decision criterion.

sessions.lesson: A payoff table should say exactly what happens to money. If an entry fee is paid, gross payoff is the amount received from the game; net payoff is gross payoff minus the fee; terminal wealth is starting wealth plus net payoff. Probabilities belong to mutually exclusive outcomes and must sum to 1. Worked example: Pay a fee of 3 for a game that pays gross 8 on heads and 0 on tails, each with probability 1/2. Net payoffs are +5 and −3. From starting wealth 20, terminal wealth is 25 or 17. Guided check: A fee of 2 buys a draw with gross payoffs 6,2,0 having probabilities .25,.50,.25. Write gross payoff, net payoff and terminal wealth from 30.

sessions.lesson: For finite net payoffs x_i with probabilities p_i, expected net payoff is Σp_i x_i. Every mutually exclusive payoff state must be included. EV is a long-run/probability-weighted average, not a promise about one play. Worked example: A game has net +6 with probability .30 and net −2 with probability .70. EV=.30(6)+.70(−2)=0.4. A single play still gives either +6 or −2. Guided check: Compute EV for net +4 with probability .40, +1 with .20 and −3 with .40.

sessions.purpose: Connect expectation to a precise break-even price without importing market-pricing theory.

sessions.lesson: If a game has gross payoff G and deterministic entry fee f, net payoff is G−f, so E[net]=E[G]−f. A fair entry fee in the narrow EV sense solves E[net]=0, hence f=E[G]. This is a mathematical break-even price, not a claim about anyone's preferences. Worked example: Gross payoffs 12,4,0 occur with probabilities .25,.50,.25. E[G]=3+2=5, so the EV-fair fee is 5. At fee 6, EV is −1. Guided check: Gross payoff 10 with probability .3 and 2 otherwise. Find the EV-fair fee.

sessions.lesson: For net +a on success and −b on failure, E=pa−(1−p)b. Break-even solves pa−(1−p)b=0, giving p*=b/(a+b). The failure probability must remain 1−p. Worked example: Win +9 or lose −3. Break-even p solves 9p−3(1−p)=0, so p=1/4. Guided check: Find the break-even success probability for +6 versus −2.

sessions.lesson: Break-even can solve for any one unknown if the other model inputs are fixed. If a fee f is always paid and gross prize x occurs with probability p, with zero gross otherwise, E[net]=px−f. Break-even prize is x=f/p. Raising a deterministic fee by 1 lowers EV by exactly 1; it does not change p. Worked example: Fee 5, prize x with probability .25, zero otherwise gives EV=.25x−5 and break-even x=20. Guided check: Fee 3 and success probability .60; find the break-even gross prize.

sessions.lesson: In a 2×2 adversarial payoff matrix, each cell is the row player's payoff for one row/column action pair. If the column player minimizes that payoff, row best responses maximize within a column and column best responses minimize within a row. Worked example: [[2,0],[1,3]]. Against left, row chooses top(2>1); against right, bottom(3>0). Column minimizes top at right(0) and bottom at left(1), so there is no cell that is both responses. Guided check: Analyze [[1,2],[0,3]].
